title: India Walks Fine Line on Dollar Dominance as BRICS Summit Eyes Cross-Border Payment Links
excerpt: The RBI has proposed linking BRICS members' digital currencies for trade and tourism payments ahead of the New Delhi summit on September 12-13, while insisting the effort is not aimed at de-dollarisation.
body:
• The Reserve Bank of India has proposed linking BRICS members' central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) for cross-border trade and tourism payments — the first such proposal within the bloc — ahead of the September 12-13 summit in New Delhi.
  • India has framed the push as a way to cut transaction costs and boost trade, explicitly distancing it from any attempt at de-dollarisation, even as the effort could reduce reliance on the dollar as an intermediary currency.
  • BRICS Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors met in Jaipur on August 12-13 to advance fast payment system and CBDC linkages, with a follow-up meeting planned for early September.
  • US President Trump has warned of 100% tariffs on BRICS exports if the bloc tries to replace the dollar, raising the diplomatic stakes for India as summit host.

When heads of state from the 11-member BRICS bloc gather in New Delhi on September 12-13, one of the most delicate items on the agenda will be a proposal that India has been careful to describe as anything but what its critics call it: a step toward de-dollarisation.

The Reserve Bank of India has recommended that BRICS countries link their official central bank digital currencies to make cross-border trade and tourism payments easier, according to two sources cited by Reuters. If adopted, it would be the first time such a proposal is formally put forward within the bloc.

The Proposal

India's plan builds on a 2025 declaration at the BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, which called for interoperability between members' payment systems. The RBI wants to connect its digital rupee — the e-rupee, which has attracted 7 million retail users since its December 2022 launch — with CBDCs from other BRICS nations, including China's digital yuan and Brazil's pilot digital real.

The mechanics are complex. For the linkages to work, members would need to agree on interoperable technology platforms, governance rules, and mechanisms to handle trade imbalances. One idea under discussion involves bilateral foreign exchange swap arrangements between central banks, with weekly or monthly settlements, according to the Reuters sources.

"The aim of this discussion is to look at practical mechanisms to reduce transaction costs for bilateral trade. These discussions are not framed against country A, country B, or grouping A, grouping B; they stand on their own footing."

— Indian official, speaking to The Hindu BusinessLine

Why India Is Threading the Needle

India's careful framing is no accident. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called the BRICS alliance "anti-American" and threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on exports from BRICS countries if they attempt to replace the US dollar in global trade. As summit host, India faces the task of advancing financial cooperation among members — several of whom are under US sanctions — without provoking a trade backlash from Washington.

Officials have sought to draw a clear line between cross-border payment efficiency and currency replacement. "India has projected these as a way to cut transaction costs and boost trade and investment, rather than as an alternative to global payment systems, or an attempt at de-dollarisation," The Hindu BusinessLine reported, citing sources.

India has already established bilateral cross-border payment integration with the UAE and is working on similar systems with Russia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Ethiopia. The UPI-Singapore link, operational since early 2025, serves as a template.

Past Roadblocks

Previous efforts to conduct more trade in local currencies have stumbled. Russia accumulated large balances of Indian rupees from oil trade for which it found limited use, forcing the RBI to permit the investment of such balances in Indian bonds — an awkward workaround that highlighted the structural challenges of bypassing dollar-based settlement.

Hesitation among BRICS members to adopt technology platforms from other countries could also delay progress, one of the Reuters sources cautioned. Consensus on tech standards and regulation would be needed before any concrete linkage materializes.

The Broader Picture

The BRICS Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors track met in Jaipur on August 12-13 and is expected to reconvene in early September to finalize proposals on CBDC and fast payment system linkages for the summit. A parallel event — the iBRICS investor summit — will feature closed-door discussions on non-dollar settlement corridors and capital deployment targets, according to ANI.

While interest in CBDCs has been dampened globally by the rise of stablecoins, India continues to position the e-rupee as a safer, more regulated alternative. "CBDCs do not pose many of the risks associated with stablecoins," RBI Deputy Governor T. Rabi Sankar said last month, citing concerns about monetary stability and illicit payments.

What's Next

The summit itself will unfold against the backdrop of the West Asia crisis, escalating US tariff pressures, and intensifying competition between dollar-based and alternative financial infrastructure. Whether the CBDC linkage proposal gains enough consensus among all 11 members — which now include Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Indonesia alongside the original five — will be an early indicator of how far BRICS is willing to go in building parallel financial rails, and how far India is willing to lead that charge without calling it what many believe it is.
nri_angle: Cross-border CBDC linkages could lower remittance costs and speed up fund transfers for millions of Indians abroad, building on existing UPI integrations with Singapore and the UAE.
